patch.objective: Screen for sepsis and recognize septic, anaphylactic and hypovolemic shock

sources.cite: Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026. Crit Care Med 2026;54(4) (published 2026-03-23); also Intensive Care Med 2026, doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult case sepsis-to-septic-shock, not re-read for this band; its note: Supersedes 2021 where they differ. As relayed by secondary summaries read 2026-11-10 (Epocrates; Critical Care Update 2026-04-30; clinical-database.com Part 3): septic shock antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h; crystalloids first line (strong) and balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline (conditional); about 30 mL/kg initially kept (algorithm figure: at least 30 mL/kg within 3 h); serial lactate (Rec 51) and capillary refill time as an adjunct (Rec 52) to guide resuscitation; norepinephrine first line (Rec 53, strong); vasopressin added on escalating norepinephrine (Rec 56); MAP about 65 managed as a range, 60-65 suggested at age 65 or older; figure: start the vasopressor peripherally if there is no central access, and it may start with fluids in unstable shock. The primary text was not opened (the publisher page refused the fetch); confirm recommendation numbers and wording at the next review.

sources.cite: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49(11):e1063-e1143. doi:10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult case sepsis-to-septic-shock, not re-read for this band; its note: Used for: antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h, for possible septic shock or a high likelihood of sepsis (strong); within 3 h for possible sepsis without shock if concern persists (weak); at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 h for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion; initial MAP target 65 mmHg; norepinephrine first line; starting a vasopressor peripherally rather than delaying until central access; guiding resuscitation by lactate. Checked through a secondary listing (WikEM, Sepsis (main), read 2026-11-10); the primary text was not opened this session.

sources.cite: Levy MM, Evans LE, Rhodes A. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Bundle: 2018 update. Crit Care Med 2018;46(6):997-1000 (the Hour-1 bundle)
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult case sepsis-to-septic-shock, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-16 in the paper's full text (a copy posted by Universidade Federal do Paraná; summarizing fetch with quotes); first listed from WikEM on 2026-11-10. Table 1: 'Measure lactate level. Re-measure if initial lactate is > 2 mmol/L'; 'Obtain blood cultures prior to administration of antibiotics'; 'Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics'; 'Rapidly administer 30mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L'; vasopressors to 'maintain mean arterial pressure ≥ 65mm Hg'. The text says an elevated lactate is 'remeasured within 2−4h', so the 2-4 h wording is the paper's own.

sources.cite: Singer M, Deutschman CS, Seymour CW, et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315(8):801-810
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult case sepsis-to-septic-shock, not re-read for this band; its note: Septic shock: sepsis needing a vasopressor to hold MAP at 65 or more with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid. Stated from the published definition; not re-opened this session.
